title: Fitting plasterboard dry lining to a masonry wall
subtitle: Fix plasterboard sheets to a brick or block wall using adhesive dabs or battens to create a skim-ready internal surface
excerpt: How to fix plasterboard dry lining to a masonry wall. Covers preparing the wall, cutting boards to size, fixing with adhesive dabs or timber battens, taping joints, and applying jointing compound to a paint-ready finish.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). British Gypsum White Book technical guidance (open access). UK trade practice for dry-lining installation.

glossaryTerms.definition: A method of fixing plasterboard to masonry using blobs of plasterboard adhesive applied in a grid pattern directly onto the wall. The board is pressed onto the dabs and held in position until the adhesive grips. The dabs leave a 10-25 mm air cavity behind the board that allows moisture movement.

A method of finishing internal masonry walls using plasterboard sheets rather than wet plaster coats. The boards can be skim-plastered or taped and filled with jointing compound to give a flat, paint-ready surface without the drying time of sand-and-cement render.

content.text: Dry lining fixes plasterboard sheets to a masonry wall using adhesive dabs or timber battens to give an insulated, skim-ready surface without full wet plaster. The method avoids the long drying time of sand-and-cement render. INTERMEDIATE: measuring, cutting, and handling large boards with one helper is the main demand.

The masonry must be dry and structurally sound. Repair any serious cracks before lining. Switch off and isolate any electrical circuits in the wall, and cap cables that will be buried behind the boards. Mark the positions of buried conduit, pipe runs, and socket boxes on the wall face before they disappear.

Score the paper face of the plasterboard with a utility knife along a straight batten, then snap the board over a batten placed under the score line. Cut the backing paper at the fold to separate. Boards cut on the taper edge should be positioned at joints; cut edges go to corners or floor level where they will be concealed or covered by coving.

adhesive in blobs about 50 mm in diameter at 400 mm centres in a grid across the wall area, with a continuous ribbon along the top, bottom, and side edges. Press the board onto the dabs, align it with a spirit level, and check the face plane against adjacent boards using a long straight batten.

On very uneven masonry, fix 50 x 25 mm treated softwood battens to the wall at 400 or 600 mm centres, packing them out where needed to achieve a flat plane. Screw the boards to the battens at 300 mm intervals using
screws, countersinking just below the paper face.

Apply self-adhesive scrim tape along all board joints. Apply the first coat of jointing compound over the tape with the taping knife, pressing firmly to embed the tape. Allow to dry overnight, then apply a second wider coat, feathering 200 to 300 mm either side of the joint. Sand lightly when fully dry. A third thin coat gives the flattest finish before painting or skimming.

attrs.cause: Adhesive dabs were too small, too far apart, or the board was not pressed firmly when fixed.
attrs.fix: Re-fix by injecting additional adhesive through small holes drilled in the board face, pressing the board flat, then filling the holes.

attrs.symptom: Jointing compound cracks at board joints after painting
attrs.cause: The joint was not taped, or only one thin coat of compound was applied before painting.
attrs.fix: Open the crack with a scraper, apply scrim tape, and apply at least two feathered coats of compound, allowing full drying between coats.

attrs.symptom: Damp patches appear through the board after a few months
attrs.cause: The masonry behind had an active leak or persistent damp that was not resolved before lining.
attrs.fix: Remove the affected boards, diagnose and fix the moisture source, allow the masonry to dry fully, then relay the boards.
